messages.subject: Quick question about parameters convergence
parts:
Hi all!

Thanks in advance to anyone taking the time to read this question. It is a quick and naive one.

When working with capture-recapture models when survival or any other parameter (recapture, transition probability etc) is determined by other parameters such as sex or a random effect of time, example (simplified):

logit(phi[i,t]) <- beta[sex[i] + epsilon[t]
phi_female[t] <- ilogit(beta[2] + epsilon[t]

I wonder which we should check for convergence (my first thought is to check all).

For example, when I look at phi plots, R-hats ( ~ 1, 1.01), n.eff (more than 1,000), good mixing, everything indicates nice convergence but when I go down to beta and epsilon things look a little bit uglier: lower n.eff, higher R-hats.

I checked this with my own dataset and also with the simpler dipper dataset and I don't know if there is any logical explanation and it is unavoidable or if it is indicating to me any problem with my data!

I hope I explained myself clearly.

Thank you


Iraida

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Quick question about parameters convergence
parts:
Hey Iraida,

Let me try to answer your question with a recent application I had. I did a multisite capture-recapture model with just three sites. I wanted to partial pool the parameters across sites, so I specified random site effects for survival, state transitions, and recapture. I did this because I didn't want the model to estimate all parameters separately for each site without the model 'knowing' what's happening for these parameters at the other sites. So for phi, I specified:

for(m in 1:n.site){
   phi.eps[m] ~ dnorm(0, sd = phi.sigma)
   logit(phi[m]) <- phi.alpha + phi.eps[m]
}

However, knowing that I had only three sites, I wasn't actually interested in the hyperparameters (phi.alpha and phi.sigma), because a huge range of values in each parameter could explain my observations of only three sites. For this reason as well, the parameters phi.alpha and phi.sigma don't mix well and don't really converge. However, when I monitor phi[m], the site-specific parameters, I get perfect convergence. So the model is able to converge on your site-level parameters but not the hyperparameters governing them. In my case this is fine; I wanted to partial pool to get "better" estimates for the site-specific parameters, but I wasn't interested in inferring larger trends from the hyperparameters.

I haven't seen much written about this stuff, and I'd love to know if other people have thoughts as well. However, from my experience, it's OK if some parameters don't converge. Just don't make inferences on these parameters, and make sure the parameters you're actually interested in (in my case, the site-specific parameters) do converge.

Hope this helps a little.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Quick question about parameters convergence
parts:
Hi Iraida,

I'm not seeing enough of your model to know (and having a bit of trouble interpreting the code you did give because there are missing parentheses/brackets and both "phi" and "phi_female"), but if random effects and fixed effects are not mixing. it is often because either or both of them trade off with an overall intercept. Sometimes you can do simple things like subtracting off the mean of a covariate or reparameterizing in some fashion. Or sometimes you can use samplers that jointly sample highly-correlated parameters. 

Others may have specific suggestions for the type of model you are using.

-chris
